evidence.note: Systematic, targeted RFC reading before/while implementing: grepped and sed-extracted literals headers, predefined FSE distributions, sequence code tables, Huffman, dictionary format, and Appendix A tables into /tmp files for reliable reference — section-by-section work well above skimming.

Built a custom parse_zst.c and used od/xxd on real .zst artifacts to inspect actual frame/block/literals/sequence byte layouts — genuine format reconnaissance grounding understanding in observed bytes.

Repeatedly returned to RFC for FSE sequence state-init order and bitstream reading order, but mis-read the tricky details (dummy-row table shift, LSB-vs-MSB padding marker) — comprehension of the hardest subsystem stayed wrong; reading was reactive-after-failure, not verified-before-trusting.

Discovered its hard-coded default LL/ML/OF normalized distributions were 'definitely wrong' and went back to RFC to fix them — confirming an imperfect initial model of field values that anchor 8 would require getting right up front.

Wrote the whole decoder in one shot from a partially-assembled model, then never converged on correct FSE/bit-order comprehension, abandoning to dlopen(libzstd) — the RFC model never became precise/verified for the trickiest areas.

reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it read the RFC section-by-section before/while implementing and examined actual byte layouts more than 'occasionally' (custom parser + od/xxd on real frames). But it falls short of anchor 8, which requires extracting the exact rules for the tricky areas (FSE table build, bitstream bit-ordering, default distributions) and cross-checking them against hex dumps *before trusting* the implementation. Here the byte-checking was reactive after failures, and the readings of bit-ordering and FSE construction remained subtly wrong throughout, never converging. That places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.
